notes.meaning: Outcast tax collectors and notorious sinners crowded around Jesus to hear His teaching. They were drawn by His welcoming words and message of hope. Tax collectors worked for the Roman empire and were despised by their fellow Jews as dishonest traitors.

The religious leaders grumbled that Jesus welcomed these outcasts and even ate meals with them. In that culture, sharing a meal was a clear sign of friendship and acceptance. The scribes and Pharisees thought a true holy teacher should stay away from corrupt people.

Jesus answered their complaints by telling them parables. These stories form one single teaching about God's heart for lost people. He wanted to show how heaven rejoices whenever a sinner is brought home.

Jesus asked His hearers to picture a shepherd who loses one sheep out of a flock of one hundred. A shepherd does not simply write off the missing sheep, because a lost sheep is defenseless and unable to find its own way back. He leaves the other ninety-nine in the pasture and searches diligently until he finds it.

When the shepherd finds the weary sheep, he does not beat it or force it to walk. Instead, he joyfully hoists it onto his own shoulders to carry it home. This shows the tender strength of Christ in rescuing helpless sinners.

When the shepherd arrives home, his joy is too great to keep to himself. He gathers his friends and neighbors together so they can celebrate with him. Finding what was lost is meant to be shared by the whole community.

Jesus explains that heaven erupts with deep joy whenever one sinner repents. Repentance means turning from sin back to God. That joy is far greater than over many people who think they are already righteous and do not need to repent.

differ.view: Some Baptists see the ninety-nine as self-righteous religious leaders left in their spiritual lostness, rather than truly holy people.
Methodists understand the ninety-nine as believers who have lived upright lives and do not need the radical turning from gross sin that open outcasts do.

notes.meaning: Jesus then describes a woman who has ten silver coins and misplaces one in her house. Because the coin is valuable to her, she lights a lamp, sweeps the floor, and searches eagerly until she finds it. This illustrates how earnestly God seeks after every lost soul.

As soon as she recovers the coin, she calls her friends and neighbors together to rejoice. Finding what was lost turns distress into open celebration. True joy naturally wants others to share in the gladness.

Jesus repeats that there is joy in the presence of God's angels over even one repentant sinner. God Himself rejoices over the recovered soul, and all of heaven shares in His delight. This directly rebuked the Pharisees, who grumbled at the very thing that made God glad.

Jesus begins a third story about a father and his two sons. The father pictures God, who shows patient love toward different kinds of people. The two sons represent two distinct ways people stray from God's heart.

The younger son boldly demands his share of the family inheritance before his father has even died. This showed a selfish desire for independence, treating the father as if he were already gone. With great patience, the father grants the request and divides the estate between both sons.

Within a few days, the younger son turns his share into money and travels to a distant country far from home. There he wastes all his wealth on reckless, wild living. Sin often begins with an urge to get away from God's loving guidance.

Just as the son runs out of money, a severe famine sweeps through the whole country. Having spent everything, he suddenly finds himself in desperate need. Worldly pleasures leave the soul empty and helpless when trouble strikes.

To survive, the young man hires himself out to a local citizen who sends him into the fields to feed pigs. For Jewish listeners, working with unclean pigs was the most shameful and degrading job possible. Sin drags a person into spiritual poverty and misery.

The young man is so starved that he longs to eat the carob pods fed to the swine. Yet in that strange land, not a single person gives him anything. His fair-weather friends are gone, leaving him completely abandoned.

At his lowest point, the son finally comes to his senses and sees his foolishness clearly. He remembers that even the daily workers on his father's estate have more than enough bread to eat. Realizing he is dying of hunger, he begins to appreciate the goodness of the home he left behind.

The young man resolves to return home and confess his wrongdoing to his father. He understands that his rebellion was first of all a sin against God in heaven, as well as against his earthly father. True repentance always starts with an honest admission of guilt.

The son recognizes that he has forfeited any right to family status. He decides to ask only to be hired as a daily worker so he can survive. He returns with genuine humility, expecting nothing but hoping for mercy.

The son heads home, but while he is still far off, his father spots him and is filled with deep compassion. The father runs to his ragged child, throws his arms around his neck, and kisses him repeatedly. This moving picture shows God's eager readiness to welcome any sinner who returns to Him.

The son speaks his confession, admitting his sin against heaven and his father, and saying he is no longer worthy to be called a son. However, he never finishes his planned request to become a hired hand. The father's loving embrace interrupts his fears and restores him as a child of the house.

The father commands the servants to bring out the finest robe, put a ring on his finger, and place sandals on his feet. The robe covers his filthy rags, the ring restores family authority, and the sandals show he is a free son rather than a barefoot slave. God fully cleanses and restores those who return to Him.

The father orders that the specially fattened calf, reserved for great occasions, be slaughtered for a feast. The return of the broken son calls for celebration throughout the whole household. God takes great delight in welcoming His lost children back into fellowship.

The father explains why they must feast: his son was spiritually dead, but is now alive again; he was lost, but is found. Turning back to God is like rising from the dead into a brand-new life. The entire household joins together in sincere rejoicing.

Meanwhile, the older son returns from working hard in the fields. As he nears the house, he hears the sound of festive music and dancing. This hardworking son represents the religious leaders who took pride in their outward obedience.

Instead of going inside, the older son calls one of the servants and asks what the celebration is about. He is surprised and suspicious of the sudden party. He turns to a servant for answers rather than going directly to his father.

The servant explains that his younger brother has come home safe and sound. Because he has returned in good health, the father has killed the fattened calf to celebrate. The household views the brother's safe return as a wonderful blessing.

The older brother becomes furious and refuses to step inside the house. His father comes outside and gently pleads with him to join the feast. This shows God's patient love even toward proud, bitter, and self-righteous people.

The older son angrily boasts of his many years of hard labor and strict obedience. He complains that he was never even given a young goat to hold a party with his friends. He viewed his relationship with his father like a slave working for wages rather than a loved son.

In his bitter resentment, the older brother refuses to call the younger man his brother, referring to him coldly as 'this son of yours.' He accuses his brother of squandering the family property with prostitutes and grumbles that he received a feast anyway. A legalistic spirit assumes the worst of others and resents the grace shown to them.

The father replies tenderly, reminding the older son that he has always enjoyed his father's presence and fellowship. Since the estate had already been divided, everything remaining in the home belonged to the older son. God's grace to returning sinners takes nothing away from those who have always walked with Him.

The father insists that it was necessary to rejoice because a lost family member has returned to life. He gently corrects the older son by calling the young man 'this brother of yours.' Jesus leaves the story open-ended, challenging the Pharisees to choose whether they will enter God's celebration or stay outside in bitterness.
